title: Zechariah 5:1–4
context: Zechariah 5:1–4 is the sixth night vision in the common count. The prophet sees a flying scroll twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide, and the interpreting angel explains it as “the curse that goes out over the surface of the whole land” (5:3). The scroll names two offenders, everyone who steals and everyone who swears falsely, and the LORD of Armies says the curse will enter the house of the thief and of the one who swears falsely by his name and destroy it, timber and stones (5:3–4). These recall the commands against misusing the LORD’s name and against stealing (Exodus 20:7 and 20:15; Deuteronomy 5:11 and 5:19), and Leviticus 19:11–12 sets stealing and swearing falsely by the LORD’s name side by side. The curse belongs with the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 27–28. Some readers take the two offenses as representing the whole law, one toward God and one toward neighbor; others read them as two prominent sins in the community of that time. Some readers also note that the scroll’s measurements match the porch of Solomon’s temple in 1 Kings 6:3, but the significance of the size is uncertain. Historic, symbolic, and future readings appear in both traditions. Shared ground: the LORD who restores his people also purges sin from the land.

verses.text: Then again I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a flying scroll.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet lifts up his eyes again and sees a flying scroll. Arminian readers note that a scroll suggests a written word, and they hear in its flight a message that goes out openly to the whole land, warning before it judges.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image and read the scroll as the LORD’s written law carried out with authority. Shared ground: both traditions read the flying scroll as God’s word of judgment moving through the community, not as a mysterious object to be decoded.

verses.text: He said to me, “What do you see?” I answered, “I see a flying scroll; its length is twenty cubits, and its width ten cubits.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet reports the scroll’s size, twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide. Arminian readers see the size as making the message impossible to miss, and they note that some readers compare the measurements of the temple porch in 1 Kings 6:3.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same comparison and hold it loosely, since the vision does not explain the measurements. Shared ground: both traditions read the large, open scroll as a public word, visible to all the land and addressed to every household in it.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “This is the curse that goes out over the surface of the whole land, for everyone who steals shall be cut off according to it on the one side; and everyone who swears falsely shall be cut off according to it on the other side.
verses.arminianNotes: The angel explains the scroll as the curse going out over the whole land, cutting off everyone who steals and everyone who swears falsely. Arminian readers recall Exodus 20:15 and 20:7, with Deuteronomy 5:19 and 5:11, and they hear a call to repentance before the curse falls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 27–28 and read the two sides of the scroll as the law’s just verdict. Some readers in both traditions take the two offenses as representing the two tables of the law; others read them as two prominent sins of that time.

verses.text: I will cause it to go out,” says the LORD of Armies, “and it will enter into the house of the thief, and into the house of him who swears falsely by my name; and it will remain in the middle of his house, and will destroy it with its timber and its stones.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says the curse will enter the house of the thief and of the one who swears falsely by his name, remaining there until it destroys timber and stones. Arminian readers note that the judgment reaches each guilty household, matching the pairing in Leviticus 19:11–12.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same thoroughness and read it as the LORD purging sin from the restored community he is building. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as covenant justice, and some readers in both see a contrast with the LORD’s house being rebuilt in chapter 4.
